sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: Complete the sentence: The Indian Constitution provides legal remedies for the protection of our fundamental rights. This is called the Right to ____, given in Article ____ of the Constitution.
Fill in the blanks: (a) A practice where a person is compelled to serve without any payment is called ____. (b) No bill can become a law unless it is signed by the ____.
Complete the sentences: (I) A practice where a person is compelled to serve without any payment is called ____. (II) Selling and buying of human beings is called ____.
questions.answer: (I) begar (forced labour) (II) traffic in human beings (human trafficking)

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: Ten fundamental duties have been added in Part ____ of the Constitution under Article 51A in the year ____ through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment.
True or False: (a) Fundamental Duties are justiciable. (b) No child below 14 years can be employed in a factory, mine or hazardous work.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Under which Article was the Right to Education included in the Fundamental Rights, and why?
questions.answer: It was included as Article 21A in 2002 by the 86th Amendment, so that all children of 6–14 years (and their parents) could claim free and compulsory education as a fundamental right, a major step towards making India free of illiteracy.

or.q: In which year was the Right to Education Act passed, and what does it aim to achieve for children in India?
or.answer: It was passed in 2009. It aims to ensure that every child between 6 and 14 years who is out of school goes to school and receives free, compulsory, quality education as a right.

questions.q: Why has untouchability been made a punishable offence under law in India? Explain.
questions.answer: Untouchability denied millions of people equal status and dignity because of their caste or occupation. To uplift them socially and establish equality, the Constitution abolished it (Article 17) and made its practice in any form a punishable offence.

questions.q: When was the National Human Rights Commission established, and why was it set up?
questions.answer: It was established in 1993 by the Government of India to guarantee that Indian citizens enjoy human rights — to inquire into violations and protect the rights to life, liberty, equality and dignity recognised in the Constitution and international declarations.

questions.q: Mention any two restrictions imposed on the Right to Freedom.
questions.answer: (1) Freedom of speech and expression may be restricted in the interest of the sovereignty, integrity and security of India, public order, decency or morality, or to prevent defamation and contempt of court. (2) The freedom to assemble must be peaceful and without arms and can be restricted for public order.

or.q: Explain any two provisions of the Right against Exploitation.
or.answer: (1) Traffic in human beings, begar and other forced labour are prohibited and punishable. (2) No child below 14 years can be employed in any factory, mine or hazardous work.

questions.q: Describe the importance of human rights in the Indian Constitution.
questions.answer: Many human rights in the UN Universal Declaration (1948) — equality, life and liberty, freedom of religion, assembly and movement — are included as justiciable Fundamental Rights, so the government must protect them; others are in the Directive Principles. The NHRC (1993) safeguards them.

or.answer: (1) To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem. (2) To protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife.

questions.q: Explain the relationship between rights and duties.
questions.answer: Rights and duties are complementary: every right brings a duty to respect the same right of others. If I have the right to life, others have a duty not to harm me; if I have the right to use public places, I have the duty not to deny them to others.

questions.q: Describe any two freedoms given in the Indian Constitution.
questions.answer: (1) Freedom of speech and expression — to express views freely, subject to reasonable restrictions. (2) Freedom to move freely and reside in any part of India. (Others: to assemble peacefully, form associations, and practise any profession.)

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: How many freedoms have been provided by Article 19 of the Indian Constitution? Explain any three.
questions.answer: Six freedoms. (1) Freedom of speech and expression — to express opinions through speech, writing or media, subject to restrictions for security, public order and morality. (2) Freedom to assemble peacefully and without arms — to hold meetings and processions. (3) Freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business — subject to qualifications the State may lay down. (Also: to form associations, move freely, and reside anywhere in India.)

or.q: How many Fundamental Rights are given to Indian citizens? Explain any three.
or.answer: Six. (1) Right to Equality — equality before law, no discrimination, abolition of untouchability and titles. (2) Right against Exploitation — ban on human trafficking, begar and child labour below 14. (3) Right to Constitutional Remedies — the right to approach the Supreme Court (Article 32) if any right is violated. (Also: Right to Freedom, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights.)

questions.q: Describe the 'Right to Equality' as one of the important Fundamental Rights.
questions.answer: (1) Equality before law and equal protection of laws — no one is above the law. (2) No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; equal access to shops, wells, roads; equal opportunity in public employment, with reservation for SC, ST and OBC. (3) Untouchability is abolished and punishable, and titles like 'Sir' and 'Rai Bahadur' are abolished.

questions.q: Explain the provisions under the 'Right against Exploitation'.
questions.answer: (1) Traffic in human beings — buying and selling people, especially women and children — is prohibited. (2) Begar and other forms of forced labour are banned and punishable. (3) Children below 14 cannot be employed in factories, mines or hazardous work, so that they can enjoy childhood and get education.

questions.q: How does the Right to Freedom of Religion give every religious group freedom to manage its religious affairs? Explain.
questions.answer: Subject to public order, morality and health, every religious group may (1) establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes, (2) manage its own affairs in matters of religion, and (3) own, acquire and administer movable and immovable property according to law. The State cannot favour any religion, as India is secular.

questions.q: 'The Right to Constitutional Remedies is the most important fundamental right.' Justify.
questions.answer: (1) It makes all other rights enforceable — without it they would be mere declarations. (2) Any citizen whose right is violated can directly approach the Supreme Court (Article 32) or a High Court, which can issue writs and orders. (3) It stops the legislature and executive from curbing rights; Dr. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution.

questions.q: Explain the cultural and educational rights of minorities.
questions.answer: (1) Any minority with a distinct language, script or culture has the right to conserve it. (2) No citizen can be denied admission to a State-run or aided institution on grounds of religion, race, caste or language. (3) Religious and linguistic minorities may establish and administer educational institutions, and the State cannot discriminate against them in giving aid.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the Right to Freedom of Religion mentioned in the Indian Constitution in six points.
questions.answer: (1) India is a secular state with no official religion. (2) Every person has freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate any religion. (3) Conversion by force or allurement and inhuman practices like human/animal sacrifice and sati are not allowed; the State may restrict this right for public order, morality and health and regulate secular activities linked to religion. (4) Every religious group may set up institutions, manage its religious affairs and own property. (5) No one can be forced to pay taxes used for promoting a particular religion. (6) No religious instruction is given in institutions wholly maintained by the State, and no one can be compelled to attend religious instruction or worship elsewhere (a minor needs a guardian's consent). Foreigners also enjoy this right.

or.q: Explain any six Fundamental Duties mentioned in the Indian Constitution.
or.answer: (1) To abide by the Constitution and respect the National Flag and National Anthem. (2) To cherish the noble ideals of the freedom struggle. (3) To uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India and defend the country when called upon. (4) To promote harmony and brotherhood and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women. (5) To protect the natural environment and value our composite culture. (6) To develop scientific temper, safeguard public property, abjure violence and strive for excellence; parents must educate children of 6–14 years. They were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and are non-justiciable.

questions.q: Explain the six Fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Indian Constitution.
questions.answer: (1) Right to Equality (Art. 14–18): equality before law, no discrimination, equal opportunity in jobs, abolition of untouchability and titles. (2) Right to Freedom (Art. 19–22): six freedoms, protection in conviction, life and personal liberty, safeguards on arrest; Article 21A gives free education to 6–14-year-olds. (3) Right against Exploitation (Art. 23–24): no trafficking, begar or child labour. (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Art. 25–28). (5) Cultural and Educational Rights (Art. 29–30): minorities may conserve culture and run institutions. (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art. 32): approach the Supreme Court if rights are violated. They are justiciable but subject to reasonable restrictions.
